Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:29: In the verse David the king, peace be upon him, said in Chronicles (I Chronicles 29:15), "for we are strangers before You, and sojourners, as all our fathers were; our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope [mikveh]" — they said in Bereishit Rabbah (96:2), "our days are like a shadow" — would that it were like the shadow of a wall or the shadow of a tree; rather, like the shadow of a bird, as it is said, "for our days on earth are like a shadow." "And there is no hope" — there is none who hopes not to die; all know and say with their mouths that they will die. Abraham said (Genesis 15:2), "and I go childless"; Isaac said (ibid. 27:4), "that my soul may bless you before I die"; Jacob said (ibid. 47:30), "and I will lie with my fathers." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:30: In Tanchuma (parashat Vayelech), on the verse (Deuteronomy 31:14), "behold, your days approach to die," it says, in these words: this is what Scripture says (Proverbs 11:31), "behold, the righteous shall be repaid on earth," etc. — regarding whom was this verse said? It was said only regarding Moses the righteous, than whom there was none like him among all the prophets nor among all the sages — for the Holy One, blessed be He, testified concerning him after his death (Deuteronomy 34:10), "and there arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses" — and yet it was not within his power to save himself from death; how much more so the rest of humankind! And so David said (I Chronicles 29:15), "for we are strangers before You," etc., "our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope" — but is it not already said, "hope in the Lord"? Scripture teaches, "and there is no hope" — David said, for every human condition there is hope: a poor man, until he becomes rich; a weak man, until he becomes strong; a sick man, until he is healed; a prisoner in a house of confinement, until he is released — but for the day of death there is no hope, for even the Holy One, blessed be He, spoke with Moses face to face, and yet he could not save himself from death. And so Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 9:2), "all things come alike to all," etc. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:31: Therefore a person must return in repentance while the soul is still placed within his body, as Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (ibid. 9:10), "whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might." And our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Yalkut, Kohelet, remez 989): repent while you have your strength; while the lamp is still burning, give it oil before it goes out — once the lamp has already gone out, the oil is of no use to it at all. — end of quotation. Here it is explained that the oil for the lamp is Torah and commandments, in the manner of (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "and let oil not be lacking on your head," which I explained in the Gate of Love, chapter 4. And in a similar manner it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Balak 187a); see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:32: Further they said in the Midrash (see Midrash Tehillim), on the verse (Psalms 17:1), "hear, O Lord, the right": the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel, My children, while the gates of repentance are open, repent — for I take bribes in this world; but once I sit in judgment for the World to Come, I take no bribes, as it is said (Proverbs 6:35), "he will not regard any ransom." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:33: In this manner our sages, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Mishlei on the verse (Proverbs 6:6), "go to the ant, you sluggard": Rabbi Yehudah said, the wicked are destined to say before the Holy One, blessed be He, leave us and we shall repent, and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers them: fools of the world, this world is like the eve of the Sabbath, and the World to Come is like the Sabbath — if a person does not prepare on the eve of the Sabbath, what will he eat on the Sabbath? And likewise it is like the sea and dry land — if he does not gather from the dry land, he has nothing to eat at sea. And likewise it is like the days of summer and the days of the rains — if he does not plow and sow and reap in the days of summer, what will he eat in the days of the rains? He should have learned from the ant, as it is said, "go to the ant, you sluggard."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:34: Another interpretation: this ant has neither officer nor ruler, but rather does everything through its own wisdom, and you have not learned from it out of your laziness and foolishness, and have not repented; therefore Solomon said (Proverbs 6:9), "how long will you lie there, O sluggard?" — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:35: In another version I found, after the three matters mentioned regarding this world and the World to Come, it further says: the world you have been in is like an antechamber, and the World to Come is like a banquet hall; prepare yourself in the antechamber so that you may enter the banquet hall.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:36: In Devarim Rabbah (5:2), and brought there in the Yalkut (Mishlei, siman 938, p. 134b), in the explanation of Scripture, it says that the ant lives only six months, and all its food is a grain and a half, and it says, there was an incident where they found a chamber of an ant's nest with three hundred kor of grain; therefore Solomon said, prepare for yourself commandments in this world for the World to Come. What is "consider her ways and be wise"? The proper conduct within it, that it flees from theft — Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta said: there was an incident with an ant that dropped a single grain of wheat, and all the other ants came and smelled it, but not one of them took it; the one to whom it belonged came and took it. Even so, it has neither judge nor officer, as it is said, "which has no chief, officer, or ruler" — you, who have appointed officers for yourselves, all the more so should have judges and officers! Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, this man is pitiable, who must learn from the ant — had he learned and acted, he would be pitiable [in a lesser sense]; but rather he needs to learn from her ways and has not learned. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:37: It is fitting that one hasten greatly in the deed of service, and of this it is said (Avot 2:15), "the day is short and the work is much." And so they said in the Gemara (Ketubot 67b), "the provisions are light and the journey is long" — for a one-year journey one must prepare a month or two months' worth of food; for a journey of many years after death, how much more must be prepared!
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:38: Further they said (see Shabbat 30a) on the verse (Psalms 88:6), "free among the dead" — Rabbi Yochanan said, once a person dies, he becomes free of the commandments — and this is what David meant in saying (ibid. 115:17), "the dead do not praise the Lord": a person should always engage in Torah and commandments before he dies, for once he dies he is nullified from the commandments and from the Torah, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has no praise from him. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:39: The repentance that is accepted is that done in one's youth, as Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "and remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" — and our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah, ad loc.): we have learned, Akavia ben Mahalalel says, contemplate three things and you will not come to sin — know from where you came, and to where you are going, etc. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Levi: all three are derived from a single word, "borecha" [your Creator] — "be'ercha" [your putrid drop], "boryecha" [your worm and maggot], "bor'echa" [your Creator, the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:40: "In the days of your youth" — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar taught: while you still find and are able. "Before the evil days come" — these are the days of old age. "And the years arrive of which you will say, I have no delight in them" — these are the days of the Messiah, which have neither merit nor guilt. "Before the sun darkens" — this is the forehead, etc. — end of quotation, as pertains here. And in Vayikra Rabbah (parashah 18) this passage is brought, and it says there regarding "in the days of your youth" — in the days of your childhood, while your vigor is still upon you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:41: Further, they said in Tractate Avodah Zarah, first chapter (19b), on the verse (Psalms 112:1), "happy is the man who fears the Lord," in these words: "happy is the man," and not "happy is the woman" — Rav Amram said in the name of Rav, happy is he who repents while he is [still] a man [i.e., young and strong]. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, happy is he who overcomes his inclination like a man. — end of quotation. Rashi explained "while he is a man" as, while he is young in his strength — that is, he hastens to recognize his Creator before the days of old age, like a mighty man. — end of quotation. The difference between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rav is that according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, even an old man who repents and overcomes his inclination like a young man is happy, while according to Rav, this applies specifically when he is young.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:42: So too they explained in the Zohar (parashat Kedoshim 87b) on the verse "before the hoary head you shall rise" (Leviticus 19:32), in these words: we have further learned that this verse comes for exposition — "before the hoary head you shall rise," as the colleagues have already noted regarding it — a warning to a person, before he becomes old [with gray hair], to establish himself well in the world, for it is fitting that he adorn himself at the end of his days — for there is no praise for a person when he is old and cannot be evil, but rather his praise is when he is in his full strength and is good. Solomon the king cried out and said (Proverbs 2:11), "even in his actions a youth makes himself known," etc. In this manner it is written (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "and remember your Creator in the days of your youth," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:43: Similarly they said in the Midrash (Zuta, Kohelet ch. 12): "for childhood and youth are vanity" (Ecclesiastes 11:10) — Rabbi Yitzchak said, the things a person does in his youth blacken his face in his old age. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:44: In Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Pinchas 227b) they wrote another reason for the matter of returning in repentance in the days of one's youth. It says there that there is a thin shell on a walnut, such that when the walnut is moist, it separates from the kernel easily — and this alludes to the evil inclination. They said, of blessed memory: this shell is like the shell that clings to the kernel of the nut, and when the nut is soft, that shell separates from the kernel of the nut without difficulty, but when the nut is dry, it is hard for a person to remove it from there, since the hardness still stands in its place. Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, commands a person to return in repentance in his youth, before the evil inclination grows old within him — this being what is written, "before the hoary head [seivah] you shall rise" — before your own hoary head. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:45: This is what Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 29:21), "he who pampers his servant from youth, in the end he will become a master [manon]." This servant is the evil inclination, which is a slave of slaves; and if in one's youth he pampers it with the pleasures of the world, in the end "it will become a master [manon]" — a ruler over him, and it will be hard for him to subdue it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:46: The fifth exhortation to repentance is the matter of the herald who proclaims above, every day, regarding repentance, and this is explained in several places in the Zohar, particularly in parashat Lech Lecha (77a), where it says that at midnight, when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to the lower Garden of Eden, a herald cries out with force and says: to you speak the holy supernal ones — which of you lets a spirit enter his ears, etc.; woe to those who sleep the sleep in their graves, who do not know and do not perceive where they will stand at the judgment of reckoning — [reckoning] is decreed when the body is defiled and the soul wanders over the face of the noonday air, ascending and descending, and the gates are not opened, and they roll about among stones in a sling — woe to them, who will seek them, that they not stand in this delight, in the midst of places of delight of the righteous, whose places are recorded, [while these] are handed over into the hand of Dumah, descending and not ascending — of them it is written (Job 7:9), "as a cloud vanishes and is gone, so he who goes down to Sheol shall not come up." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:47: Further, in parashat Vayetze (161b, in Sitrei Torah), in these words: the voice of the herald that is aroused from above to below — we stand with open eyes — the wheel turns from above in several directions, a sound of sweetness; awaken, you who sleep, who slumber in your graves, who do not know, do not perceive, and do not see! Ears are sealed, hearts are heavy — they sleep and do not know; Torah stands before them, and they do not attend nor know what they are gazing at — they see and do not see. Torah raises her voice: consider, you fools, open your eyes and know! There is none who attends, none who inclines his ear, until — how long will you remain within the darkness of your will? Consider, in order to know, and the light shall be revealed to you that shone at the time complete Jacob, out of the distress of the land and another dominion, among foreign grades, pushed away all of them and chose the portion of his lot and his inheritance — light out of darkness, wisdom out of foolishness — and he honored his Master when he stood under the dominion of another god. Regarding this (Isaiah 29:22), "Jacob shall not now be ashamed, nor shall his face now turn pale." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:48: Further, in the Zohar (parashat Miketz 203b), in these words: come and see, every single day, when the light rises, a certain bird awakens on a tree in the Garden of Eden, and calls out three times, and the scepter is raised, and a herald cries out with force: to you speak the mighty ones of your Master — which of you sees and does not see, who stand in the world and do not know for what purpose they stand, and do not attend to the honor of their Master; the Torah stands before them and they do not engage in it; it would be better for them not to have been created — for what purpose do they stand without understanding? Woe to them, when the days of evil come upon them and drive them out of the world. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:49: In parashat Terumah (130b), the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained the daily proclamation of repentance, in these words: it is written (Isaiah 21:12), "the morning comes, and also the night; if you will inquire, inquire; return, come" — this verse is applied to the exile of Israel who dwell among the sons of Seir, and Israel say to the Holy One, blessed be He: watchman, what of the night — what will become of us in this exile, resembling the darkness of night? What is written? "The watchman said" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He; "the morning comes" — already light has shone for everyone, and I have raised you up to My service, so that you might merit eternal life, [but] you have abandoned My Torah; "and also the night" — I have brought you into exile as before; "if you will inquire, inquire" — as it is said (Isaiah 34:16), "seek out from the book of the Lord and read" — and there you will find on what your exile depends, and your redemption, and when you inquire of it, it will say and proclaim before you, "return, come" — return in complete repentance, and immediately, come and draw near to Me. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:50: Further on, he gives another interpretation regarding "the watchman said, [the morning] comes," etc., in these words: "the watchman said" — this is Metatron; "the morning comes" — this is the morning prayer, which is the dominion of the day, that which rules over the night; and should you say that it comes alone, separated, male from female — behold, it is written "and also the night" — both together, and never separated from one another; and this voice cries out in these words, "the morning comes, and also the night" — both are ready for you. From here on, "if you will inquire, inquire" — if you seek your requests and return to your Master; "come" — as one ready to receive his children and have mercy on them; so too the Holy One, blessed be He, "the morning" and "also the night" cries out and says, "come." Happy is the holy people, whose Master seeks them and calls them to draw them near to Him — then the holy people seek to gather in the synagogue, and whoever arrives first is joined with the Shechinah in a single union. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:51: Here it is explicitly stated that the watchman Metatron proclaims repentance at the time of the morning prayer, saying, "the morning comes," etc., "return, come" — and likewise the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, called the dominion of the day and the dominion of the night, alluded to in the verse as "morning" and "night," proclaim and say, "return, come." This is what the Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in his words: so too the Holy One, blessed be He, "the morning" and "also the night" cried out and said, "return, come." Accordingly, the two proclamations mentioned in the verse are: one from Metatron, and one from the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah. And both are, in truth, one proclamation — for Metatron proclaims and says that the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, morning and night, call to their children and say, "return, come" — and the words of the Rashbi in saying "so too the Holy One, blessed be He, morning," etc., thus explain the verse: "so too" means that also the proclamation of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah is mentioned in the verse, that morning and night they call and say, "come."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:52: We further find ourselves taught, from the totality of the passage, that the essence of the prayer we pray is to appease our Creator, that He forgive our sins and that we return in complete repentance before Him — this being what it says, "if you will inquire, inquire" — if you will seek your petitions before the Holy King, seek — pray and return to your Master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:53: Further, we learn from the verse saying, "if you will inquire, inquire; return, come" — if you wish to ask requests of the Holy One, blessed be He, in prayer, return in repentance first, and afterward pray — for one who prays without repentance, of him it is said (Isaiah 1:12), "who has required this of you, to trample My courts?" And thus the precise wording of the verse, "if you will inquire," is understood — for it should have said simply "inquire; return, come"; why "if you will inquire"? The intent is as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:54: Further, we learn from the passage that one should not draw near to his Creator except after returning from his sins and casting away all his transgressions from himself — this being what it says, "return, come," and the Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in his words, "return in complete repentance, and immediately come and draw near to Me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:55: From the end of the passage we further learn His mercy, blessed be He, upon Israel, His treasured people, in that He says to them, "come," like one ready to receive his children and have mercy on them — and this is like the parable of a father saying to a son who has distanced himself from him, come to me, for I am ready and prepared to receive you. Who is there who would read these words and not have his uncircumcised heart humbled, to return to his Father in Heaven? Since his Father is merciful and wishes the son to draw near to Him, it is fitting that he not distance himself, Heaven forbid, and not stiffen his neck, but rather rise with alacrity from his sleep to come and plead before the Shechinah in the synagogue with tears and prayer, so that he be received — since the morning prayer is a time of favor, as explained above in the Gate of Love, chapter 11; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:56: Further, the matter of Metatron's proclamation the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained further on, regarding the verse (Isaiah 50:10), "who among you hears the voice of His servant" — he says there, regarding one who arrives early to the synagogue, that if for one day he does not come, the Holy One, blessed be He, asks after him and says, who among you fears the Lord, "hears the voice of His servant" — in these words: and we have already been aroused regarding this, on what is written (Isaiah 21:11), "one calls to me from Seir" — for grade after grade, within the grade, that Watchman calls out with force every single day, and this is "who hears the voice of His servant" — this is Metatron. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:57: The sixth exhortation to repentance — when a person reads the Books of the Prophets, he will find that all of them proclaim repentance. Hosea proclaims (14:2), "return, O Israel." Isaiah says (21:12), "if you will inquire, inquire; return, come. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds from before My eyes," etc. (1:16). Jeremiah says (3:22), "return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings" — and many similar verses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:58: Ezekiel elaborated and explained the matters of repentance more than all the prophets. He said (Ezekiel 18:21), "but if the wicked man turns from all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all My statutes, and does what is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die; none of his transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him," etc., "do I have any pleasure at all that the wicked should die, says the Lord God, and not that he should return from his ways and live?" (18:23) "cast away from you all your transgressions that you have transgressed against Me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, for why should you die" (18:31) — and our sages, of blessed memory, said, "why should you die" — for the wicked in his lifetime is called dead — and yet, "turn and live." Further, in another passage there (33:10), "son of man, say to the house of Israel: thus you have spoken, saying, our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we waste away in them, how then shall we live? Say to them: as I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn, turn from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel? And you, son of man, say to the children of your people: the righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him in the day of his transgression, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not cause him to stumble on the day he turns from his wickedness, and the righteous shall not be able to live by it in the day of his sin" — and the rest of that passage, hear it and know it for yourself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:59: Likewise, all the prophets who arose for Israel arose only to bring them back in repentance; and since their words are written before us, it is as though the prophet were alive and standing and teaching us the ways of repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:60: Of this aspect of exhortation our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Pesikta (DeRav Kahana, siman 24), on the matter of "return, O Israel" (Hosea 14:2): a parable of a province that was thrown into disorder by marauding troops, and there was in it a certain elder who warned all the people of the province — whoever heeded him was saved, and whoever did not heed him, the troops came upon him and killed him; therefore the prophet cries out and says, "return, O Israel." It was taught in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: "the hope [mikveh] of Israel is the Lord" — just as a mikveh purifies the impure, so the Holy One, blessed be He, purifies Israel through repentance; therefore Hosea warns Israel and says to them, "return, O Israel."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:61: The totality of these six exhortations to repentance that we have given, the Rashbi, peace be upon him, gathered into a short passage (Zohar, parashat Acharei Mot, end of p. 57), in these words: Rabbi Shimon said, I am astonished at the people of the world, for they have no eyes to see and no heart to attend, and they do not know nor set their hearts to contemplate the will of their Master — how do they sleep and not awaken from their sleep until that day comes that covers them with darkness and the grave, and that Master of the deposit demands a reckoning from them; and a herald cries out over them every day, and their own souls testify against them every day and night, and the Torah raises her voice on every side, proclaiming and saying (Proverbs 1:22), "how long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?" Whoever is simple, let him turn here, the lacking-hearted one — she said to him, "come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine I have mixed" (Proverbs 9:4-5) — and there is none who inclines his ear, and none whose heart is awakened. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:62: The first three exhortations that I explained are included in his words, in saying, "and they do not set their hearts to contemplate the will of their Master" — for His will, blessed be He, is that we rectify our souls, which are a part of Him, and that we repent so that we not need the refining of Gehinnom, and likewise that we rectify His Shechinah's exile. And he says, "I am astonished at the people of the world" — regarding those whose whole attention is upon the affairs of this world and not upon the affairs of the supernal world, "for they have no eyes to see" — meaning, the eyes and the heart were created within them in vain, for the eyes were essentially created so that a person might gaze through them upon spiritual matters, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 8, and the heart, to cling to the simple will that is within the Name, blessed be He, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayakhel 128b) regarding "whose heart makes him willing" — and we shall quote his words on the matter of prayer, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:63: The fourth exhortation is from the matter of the days: he says, "how do they sleep and not awaken until that day comes," etc. The fifth exhortation is from the herald: he says, "and a herald." And regarding the sixth: "the Torah raises her voice on every side" — for in the Torah is written the matter of several promises He promised through the prophets regarding repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:64: He further adds a seventh exhortation — this being the soul, which testifies against him every day, namely, the beginnings of repentant thoughts that come to a person every day — for there is no wicked person of Israel who does not have some contemplation of repentance, except that his inclination overpowers him and seduces him afterward; and likewise, at times some evil dream will arouse the soul, to awaken him to repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:65: The eighth exhortation is that it is fitting that one contemplate how many we find who repented and were accepted. First, Adam, the first man — they said in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 20): on the first day of the week Adam entered the upper waters of the Gihon until the water reached his neck, and fasted seven weeks of days, until his body became like a sieve. Adam said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of all worlds, remove my sin from me and accept my repentance, and let all generations learn that there is repentance and that You accept the repentance of the penitent. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He stretched out His right hand and removed his sin from him and accepted his repentance, as it is said (Psalms 32:5), "I acknowledge my sin to You, and my iniquity I have not hidden," etc., "You have forgiven the iniquity of my sin, Selah" — Selah, from this world, and Selah, from the World to Come. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:66: So too they said in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 18), that the first man said the psalm "A song for the Sabbath day" — for on the eve of the Sabbath he was expelled from the Garden of Eden, and the day of the Sabbath came and became a defender for the first man, etc. And it says further on: this verse (Psalms 92:2), "it is good to give thanks to the Lord" — the first man said this, so that all generations might learn that whoever acknowledges his transgressions and abandons them is saved from the judgment of Gehinnom, as it is said, "it is good to give thanks." — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:67: Further they said in Bereishit Rabbah (21:6) on "and now, lest he put forth his hand" (Genesis 3:22): Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said, this teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, opened for him an opening of repentance, as it is said, "and now, lest he put forth," and it is written (Deuteronomy 10:12), "and now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 1:68: Further, we learn in Bereishit Rabbah (22:13): "and Cain went out from before the Lord" (Genesis 4:16) — to where did he go? Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Huna bar Yitzchak: he went out joyful, in the manner of (Exodus 4:14), "and also, behold, he comes out to meet you," etc. Adam the first man met him and said to him, what was done regarding your judgment? He said to him, I repented and settled the matter. Adam began striking his own face and saying, such is the power of repentance, and I did not know it! Immediately he arose and said, "a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," etc. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
